questions.stem: Lead(II) sulfate, $ \mathrm{P b S O_{4}} $ , is an insoluble salt. It can be made as a precipitate from a solution of lead(II) nitrate, $ \mathrm{P b ( N O_{3} )_{2}} $

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify a substance that could be added to lead(II) nitrate solution to form a precipitate of lead(II) sulfate.

parts.label: a-ii
parts.text: Write a chemical equation for the reaction between lead(II) nitrate and the substance you identified in (a)(i).

parts.label: a-iii
parts.text: Outline how you would produce a pure, dry sample of lead(II) sulfate from the reaction mixture in (a)(ii).

parts.label: b
parts.text: A solution of lead(II) nitrate can be made by reacting solid lead(II) carbonate with dilute nitric acid. The equation for this reaction is: $\mathrm {P b C O} _ {3} (\mathrm {s}) + 2 \mathrm {H N O} _ {3} (\mathrm {a q}) \rightarrow \mathrm {P b} (\mathrm {N O} _ {3}) _ {2} (\mathrm {a q}) + \mathrm {C O} _ {2} (\mathrm {g}) + \mathrm {H} _ {2} \mathrm {O} (\mathrm {l})$ State two observations you would make when dilute nitric acid is added to solid lead(II) carbonate.

questions.stem: When magnesium is burned in air, it reacts with oxygen, $ \mathrm{O_{2}} $ , to form magnesium oxide, MgO A class of students investigated the relationship between the mass of magnesium burned and the mass of magnesium oxide formed. Each student was given a different mass of clean magnesium to heat. The students used the following method. Weigh a crucible and lid Place the magnesium ribbon in the crucible, replace the lid, and reweigh Heat the crucible as shown in the diagram until the magnesium burns Lift the lid from time to time until there is no sign of further reaction Allow the crucible and lid to cool and reweigh Repeat the heating, cooling and reweighing until two consecutive masses are the same Calculate the mass of magnesium oxide formed

parts.label: a
parts.text: Why is it necessary to lift the lid from time to time while heating?

parts.label: a-ii
parts.text: Why is it necessary to repeat the heating until two consecutive masses are the same?

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show how the mass of magnesium oxide formed can be calculated from the readings obtained.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The results of each experiment are given in the table.

parts.label: c-i
parts.text: Plot the results on the grid and draw a straight line of best fit.

parts.label: c-ii
parts.text: Draw a circle around the anomalous result.

parts.label: c-iii
parts.text: Use your graph to find the mass of magnesium oxide formed when 0.48 g of magnesium is burned.

parts.label: a-ii
parts.text: Identify gas A.

parts.text: Some of the solution formed after the electrolysis was tested with the indicator phenolphthalein. The indicator turned pink Explain this result.

parts.label: c-i

parts.label: c-ii

questions.stem: Compound X is a blue, crystalline solid. It contains copper(II) ions $ \mathrm{(C u^{2+})} $ , sulfate ions $ \mathrm{(S O_{4}^{2-})} $ and water of crystallisation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student dissolved some of compound X in water and then added aqueous sodium hydroxide solution. She obtained a blue precipitate. Give the formula of the blue precipitate formed in the reaction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Another student tested a solution of compound X for sulfate ions using dilute hydrochloric acid, followed by a few drops of barium chloride solution. She obtained a white precipitate. Why is the dilute hydrochloric acid necessary in this test?

parts.label: c
parts.text: The empirical formula of compound X is $ \mathrm{C u S O_{9} H_{1 0}} $ Write the formula of compound X to show its water of crystallisation.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Compound X gives a blue-green colour in a flame test. Outline how you would carry out a flame test.

parts.label: b-ii

parts.label: c-i

parts.label: c-ii

questions.stem: Sulfur dioxide, $ \mathrm{S O_{2}} $ , is used as a preservative in wine. The sulfur dioxide content of a wine can be found by titration. A chemist found that $ 2 5. 0 \mathrm{c m}^{3} $ of a sample of wine reacted with exactly $ 1 5. 0 0 \mathrm{c m}^{3} $ of 0.0010 mol/dm $ ^{3} $ aqueous iodine, $ \mathrm{I}_{2} $ (aq). The equation for the reaction is $\mathrm {S O} _ {2} (\mathrm {a q}) + \mathrm {I} _ {2} (\mathrm {a q}) + 2 \mathrm {H} _ {2} \mathrm {O} (\mathrm {l}) \rightarrow \mathrm {S O} _ {4} ^ {2 -} (\mathrm {a q}) + 2 \mathrm {I} ^ {-} (\mathrm {a q}) + 4 \mathrm {H} ^ {+} (\mathrm {a q})$

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount, in moles, of iodine in $ 1 5. 0 0 \mathrm{c m}^{3} $ of a 0.0010 mol/dm $ ^{3} $ solution.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Deduce the amount, in moles, of sulfur dioxide in $ 2 5. 0 \mathrm{c m}^{3} $ of the wine.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the concentration, in mol/dm $ ^{3} $ , of sulfur dioxide in the wine.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the concentration, in $ \mathrm{g / d m^{3}} $ of sulfur dioxide in the wine.

parts.label: e
parts.text: A concentration of sulfur dioxide that is greater than $ 0. 1 6 \mathrm{~ g / d m^{3}} $ makes wine unpleasant to drink. Use the value you have calculated in (d) to state whether the wine is drinkable.
